messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Navy Officer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 33

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the office with his shoulders squared, the habit of twenty years in the Navy still evident in his posture. At thirty-four, he looks older than his years—there's a tightness around his eyes that doesn't quite match his controlled demeanor. He's been married to Jennifer for eight years, and they live near the naval base in San Diego. He agreed to come in after Jennifer finally told him that his night terrors were affecting her sleep, that she was worried about him, that something needed to change.

The trauma happened two years ago. Marcus was stationed in the Philippines as part of a humanitarian deployment when Typhoon Haiyan made landfall. He was part of the initial response team, one of the first to move into the devastated areas. He describes the experience methodically at first—the scale of destruction, the logistics of coordinating rescue efforts, the coordination with other military units. But then his voice changes slightly when he talks about the third day, when his team found a family of four in the rubble of what had been a school. Two of them were already gone. The other two were alive but barely. He had to make decisions about triage, about resource allocation, about who got help first. He was twenty minutes away from the nearest medical facility. One of them didn't make it.

For the first several months after returning home, Marcus seemed fine. He was promoted to Lieutenant Commander. He and Jennifer talked about starting a family. He threw himself into his work with the same dedication he always had. But gradually, things began to shift. He started having trouble sleeping, waking up in a cold sweat multiple times a night. Jennifer says he sometimes calls out in his sleep, and once he grabbed her arm so hard he left bruises because he was dreaming he was pulling someone from collapsed concrete.

Now, two years later, Marcus avoids anything related to natural disasters. He won't watch the news during hurricane season. He's had to decline several social invitations because they're near the beach—being near water has become unbearable, even though he's spent his entire adult life around the ocean. When he does go to work, he's hypervigilant in a way his colleagues don't seem to understand. He's constantly scanning for problems, for things that could go wrong. His commanding officer has noticed that he's become more rigid in his command style, less collaborative than he used to be.

The worst part, Marcus says, is that he can't quite explain it to Jennifer. He'll be fine one moment, and then something small—a weather alert on his phone, a news story about flooding—will send him spiraling. His heart races. His mind floods with images from the typhoon. He feels like he's back there, like the decision he made about that family is happening again, right now, in real time. These episodes last for hours sometimes. He withdraws, becomes irritable, pushes Jennifer away even though he knows that's not what he wants. She's tried to help, but he's not sure how to let her.

He describes himself as someone who has always been able to handle difficult situations. That's what he was trained for. That's who he is as a naval officer. The fact that he can't seem to move past this, that he's still having these reactions after two years, feels like a personal failure. He's caught between the identity that has sustained him—the capable officer, the problem-solver—and the reality of what his mind and body are doing to him now.
